chapter_sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Sound is produced due to vibration of different objects.
Sound travels as a longitudinal wave through a material medium.
Sound travels as successive compressions and rarefactions in the medium.
In sound propagation, it is the energy of the sound that travels and not the particles of the medium.
Sound cannot travel through vacuum.
Sound properties such as pitch, loudness and quality are determined by corresponding wave properties (frequency, amplitude, waveform).
The audible range of hearing for average human beings is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
Sound waves with frequencies below 20 Hz are called infrasonic; above 20,000 Hz are called ultrasonic.
Ultrasound has many medical and industrial applications.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Sound is produced by vibrating objects (tuning fork, vocal cords, stretched rubber band, bells, etc.).
The human voice is produced due to vibrations of the vocal cords.
When a bird flaps its wings, the vibrating wings produce sound.
A stretched rubber band when plucked vibrates and produces sound.
All musical instruments work by making some part of the instrument vibrate.
Vibration means rapid to and fro (back and forth) motion of an object.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 11.1:
sections.aim: To demonstrate that sound is produced by vibrating objects.
sections.materials: Tuning fork, rubber pad, table tennis ball, thread, support needle.
procedure: 1. Take a tuning fork and set it vibrating by striking its prong on a rubber pad.
2. Bring it near your ear and listen.
3. Touch one of the prongs of the vibrating tuning fork with your finger.
4. Suspend a table tennis ball by a thread from a support.
5. Touch the ball gently with the prong of the vibrating tuning fork.
sections.observation: You hear a sound. When you touch the prong, you feel a tingling sensation. The suspended table tennis ball is pushed away (deflected) by the vibrating tuning fork.
sections.conclusion: Sound is produced by vibrating objects. The vibrating prong disturbs the ball, proving that the prong is in vibration.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 11.2:
sections.aim: To show that a vibrating object disturbs the surrounding medium.
sections.materials: Vibrating tuning fork, beaker or glass of water.
procedure: 1. Fill water in a beaker or a glass up to the brim.
2. Gently touch the water surface with one of the prongs of the vibrating tuning fork.
3. Dip the prongs of the vibrating tuning fork in water.
sections.observation: Touching the surface causes water ripples. Dipping the prongs causes water to splash.
sections.conclusion: The vibrating tuning fork disturbs the water, demonstrating that a vibrating object disturbs the medium around it.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 11.3:
sections.aim: To identify the vibrating parts of musical instruments.
procedure: Make a list of different types of musical instruments and discuss which part vibrates to produce sound (e.g., sitar - string, drum - membrane, flute - air column).

items.question: What is sound?
items.answer: Sound is a form of energy which produces a sensation of hearing in our ears. It is produced by vibrating objects and travels through a material medium to reach our ears.

items.question: What is vibration?
items.answer: Vibration is a kind of rapid to and fro (back and forth) motion of an object. When an object vibrates, it produces sound.

items.question: How is the human voice produced?
items.answer: The human voice is produced due to vibrations in the vocal cords. When air passes through the vocal cords, they vibrate and produce sound.

items.question: Name any two objects that produce sound and state which part vibrates.
items.answer:
1. Tuning fork - the prongs vibrate to produce sound.
2. Drum (tabla) - the stretched membrane (skin) vibrates to produce sound.

items.question: Can sound be produced without utilising energy?
items.answer: No. Sound cannot be produced without utilising energy. Every vibrating object uses energy to vibrate. For example, when we strike a tuning fork or pluck a rubber band, we use our energy to set it vibrating, and this energy is converted into sound energy.

items.question: What did Activity 11.1 (tuning fork and table tennis ball) demonstrate?
items.answer: Activity 11.1 demonstrated that sound is produced by vibrating objects. The vibrating prong of the tuning fork pushed the suspended table tennis ball away, proving that the prong was in vibration and producing sound.

items.question: Explain with an example how sound is produced by a vibrating object.
items.answer: When an object vibrates, it moves to and fro rapidly. For example, when we pluck a stretched rubber band, it moves to and fro rapidly, that is, it vibrates. This vibration disturbs the surrounding air particles and produces sound. Similarly, when a tuning fork is struck on a rubber pad, its prongs vibrate rapidly, disturbing the surrounding air and producing sound. Thus, all sounds are produced by vibrations.

items.question: Why can we produce sound without vibrating an object?
items.answer: We cannot produce sound without vibrating an object. Sound is produced only when an object vibrates. If the object does not vibrate, no disturbance is created in the surrounding medium, and hence no sound is produced. This is confirmed by all activities involving sound production - in every case (tuning fork, drum, vocal cords, rubber band) - the source is always in vibration.

items.question: What happens when a vibrating tuning fork touches the surface of water?
items.answer: When a vibrating tuning fork touches the surface of water, the water gets disturbed and ripples (waves) are formed on the surface. When the prongs are dipped deeper into water, the water splashes. This shows that the vibrating prong is in rapid to and fro motion and it disturbs the medium (water) around it, just as a vibrating object in air disturbs the air around it to produce sound.

items.question: A student strikes a bell. Describe step by step how sound reaches her ear.
items.answer:
Step 1: The student strikes the bell, causing it to vibrate (to and fro motion).
Step 2: The vibrating bell disturbs the air particles surrounding it.
Step 3: The disturbed air particles push the neighbouring air particles, which in turn push their neighbours.
Step 4: This disturbance travels through the air in the form of a sound wave (compressions and rarefactions).
Step 5: When this sound wave reaches the ear of the student, it causes the eardrum to vibrate.
Step 6: The eardrum sends signals to the brain, and the student hears the sound.

items.question: If you observe carefully the list of musical instruments, you will find that each one has a vibrating part. Identify the vibrating part and the sound produced in: (a) Sitar (b) Flute (c) Drum (d) Bell.
items.answer:
(a) Sitar: The vibrating part is the string. When the string is plucked, it vibrates and produces a musical sound.
(b) Flute: The vibrating part is the air column inside the flute. When air is blown into the flute, the air column inside vibrates and produces sound.
(c) Drum (Tabla): The vibrating part is the stretched membrane (skin) on the drum. When struck, the membrane vibrates and produces sound.
(d) Bell: The vibrating part is the metal body of the bell. When struck, the metal vibrates and produces a ringing sound.

sections.label: LIST OF SUB-TOPICS:
items: 11.2.3 Speed of Sound in Different Media

DEFINITION: The transmission of sound from the source to the listener through a medium is called propagation of sound. Sound moves through a medium from the point of generation to the listener. The substance through which sound is transmitted is called a medium. Sound can travel through solids, liquids, and gases.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Sound requires a medium (solid, liquid, or gas) to travel. It cannot travel through vacuum.
Sound is produced by vibrating objects; the vibration of the object sets the particles of the medium into vibration.
A particle of the medium in contact with the vibrating object is first displaced from its equilibrium position, then exerts force on the adjacent particle, and so on.
The disturbance travels through the medium, but the particles of the medium do not travel from the source to the listener; they only oscillate about their mean positions.
A wave is a disturbance that moves through a medium when the particles of the medium set neighbouring particles into motion.
Sound waves are mechanical waves because they require a material medium.
Sound propagates as compressions (regions of high pressure) and rarefactions (regions of low pressure) in the medium.
Compression (C): region where particles are crowded together - high pressure region.
Rarefaction (R): region where particles are spread apart - low pressure region.
Sound propagation can be visualised as density variations or pressure variations in the medium.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 11.4:
sections.aim: To demonstrate propagation of longitudinal wave using a slinky.
procedure: 1. Take a slinky and ask your friend to hold one end. You hold the other end.
2. Stretch the slinky as shown in Fig. 11.5(a).
3. Give it a sharp push towards your friend.
4. Observe the motion of a dot marked on the slinky.
sections.observation:
- When pushed, the coils in some regions come closer together (compressions) and in other regions, they spread apart (rarefactions).
- The dot on the slinky moves back and forth parallel to the direction of propagation - not forward.
- The compression travels from one end to the other.
sections.conclusion:
Sound waves are longitudinal waves. The particles of the medium oscillate parallel to the direction of wave propagation.

items.question: What is a medium in the context of sound propagation?
items.answer: The substance through which sound is transmitted is called a medium. Sound can travel through solid, liquid, and gaseous media. Sound requires a material medium and cannot travel through vacuum.

items.question: Define compression and rarefaction.
items.answer:
COMPRESSION: The region in a sound wave where the particles of the medium are crowded together is called compression. It is a region of high pressure and high density.
RAREFACTION: The region in a sound wave where the particles of the medium are spread apart is called rarefaction. It is a region of low pressure and low density.

items.question: What is a wave?
items.answer: A wave is a disturbance that moves through a medium when the particles of the medium set neighbouring particles into motion. The particles of the medium do not move forward themselves; only the disturbance (energy) travels forward.

items.question: Why are sound waves called mechanical waves?
items.answer: Sound waves are called mechanical waves because they require a material medium (solid, liquid, or gas) to travel. They cannot travel through vacuum because there are no particles to carry the disturbance.

items.question: What happens to a particle of the medium when a sound wave passes through it?
items.answer: When a sound wave passes through the medium, a particle of the medium is first displaced from its equilibrium position. It then exerts a force on the adjacent particle, displacing it. After displacing the adjacent particle, the first particle comes back to its original position. Thus each particle only oscillates about its mean position; it does not travel with the wave.

items.question: How does the dot marked on the slinky move in Activity 11.4?
items.answer: The dot on the slinky moves back and forth (to and fro) parallel to the direction of propagation of the disturbance. This shows that in a longitudinal wave, the particles oscillate along the direction of wave travel, not perpendicular to it.

items.question: Explain how sound is propagated from a vibrating tuning fork to your ear.
items.answer:
When a tuning fork vibrates, its prong moves back and forth.
- When the prong moves forward, it pushes and compresses the air particles in front of it, creating a compression (high pressure region).
- When the prong moves backward, it creates a region of low pressure called rarefaction.
- A series of alternating compressions and rarefactions is thus created in the air.
- This disturbance travels from the tuning fork to the ear in the form of a sound wave.
- When it reaches the ear, the alternating compressions and rarefactions cause the eardrum to vibrate, producing the sensation of sound.

items.question: Distinguish between the motion of a particle of the medium and the motion of a sound wave.
items.answer:
Motion of a particle of medium:
- The particle only oscillates (moves to and fro) about its mean position.
- The particle does not travel from source to listener.
- The particle moves parallel to the direction of wave propagation (longitudinal motion).

Motion of a sound wave:
- The wave (disturbance/energy) travels from the source to the listener.
- The wave moves in the direction of propagation continuously.
- The wave carries energy, not matter, from one place to another.

items.question: Explain why sound cannot travel in vacuum.
items.answer: Sound is a mechanical wave that travels by making the particles of the medium vibrate. When one particle vibrates, it disturbs the adjacent particle, which in turn disturbs its neighbour, and so on. In vacuum, there are no particles. Since there are no particles to be displaced or to carry the disturbance forward, sound cannot travel through vacuum. This is why we cannot hear sounds from space, even though explosions occur there.

items.question: A vibrating object creates alternating compressions and rarefactions in air. Explain what compressions and rarefactions are and how they are created.
items.answer:
COMPRESSION:
- When the vibrating object (e.g., prong of a tuning fork) moves forward, it pushes the air particles in front of it.
- These air particles are crowded together, forming a region of high pressure.
- This region of high pressure is called a compression (C).

RAREFACTION:
- When the vibrating object moves backward, it pulls away from the air particles in front.
- The air particles spread out, forming a region of low pressure.
- This region of low pressure is called a rarefaction (R).

As the object vibrates back and forth continuously, it creates a series of alternating compressions and rarefactions in the medium. This series of compressions and rarefactions travels through the medium as a sound wave.

items.question: Using the slinky activity (Activity 11.4), explain how a sound wave is similar to the disturbance in a slinky.
items.answer:
In Activity 11.4:
- When the slinky is pushed towards the friend's end, some coils are pushed closer together (compression) and other coils are pulled apart (rarefaction).
- The regions of compression (C) and rarefaction (R) travel from one end of the slinky to the other.
- However, the dot marked on the slinky moves back and forth (oscillates) in the direction of wave travel - it does not move to the other end.

Similarity with sound waves:
- In a sound wave, compressions and rarefactions travel through the medium, just like in the slinky.
- The air particles (like the dot on the slinky) only oscillate back and forth about their mean positions.
- The energy (disturbance) travels forward, but the particles (medium) do not.
- Both the slinky disturbance and sound are longitudinal waves - particles oscillate parallel to direction of propagation.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: In a longitudinal wave, particles oscillate parallel to the direction of wave propagation.
Sound waves in air are longitudinal waves consisting of compressions and rarefactions.
The regions where coils (or particles) are closer together are compressions (C) and where they are further apart are rarefactions (R).
Transverse waves: particles oscillate perpendicular to direction of wave propagation (e.g., water surface waves, light waves).
Sound waves cannot be transverse in gases because gases cannot sustain shear stress (transverse forces).
Light is a transverse wave but NOT a mechanical wave (it does not need a medium).
In a slinky, the longitudinal wave is visible as compressions and rarefactions travelling along the coil.

items.question: Define longitudinal waves and give one example.
items.answer: Longitudinal waves are waves in which the individual particles of the medium oscillate (move to and fro) in a direction parallel to the direction of propagation of the wave. Sound waves in air are a common example of longitudinal waves.

items.question: What is the difference between a longitudinal wave and a transverse wave?
items.answer:
LONGITUDINAL WAVE: Particles oscillate parallel to the direction of wave propagation. Example: sound waves.
TRANSVERSE WAVE: Particles oscillate perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation. Example: waves on a water surface.

items.question: Why are sound waves in air called longitudinal waves? Explain with the help of the slinky activity.
items.answer:
Sound waves in air are called longitudinal waves because the air particles oscillate parallel to the direction of propagation.
In the slinky activity (Activity 11.4):
- When a sharp push is given to the slinky, compressions and rarefactions are created.
- A dot marked on the slinky moves back and forth (to and fro) along the direction in which the disturbance travels.
- This is parallel motion (not perpendicular), confirming longitudinal nature.
Similarly, in sound waves in air, the air particles move back and forth along the direction of wave travel (compressions and rarefactions), making sound a longitudinal wave.

items.question: Describe the motion of particles when a sound wave passes through air. Why is it different from the motion of waves on a water surface?
items.answer:
Motion of particles in a sound wave (air):
- When a sound wave travels through air, the air particles oscillate back and forth (to and fro) parallel to the direction of wave propagation.
- This creates alternating compressions (crowded particles, high pressure) and rarefactions (spread particles, low pressure).
- The particles oscillate about their mean position but do not travel along with the wave.
- Sound waves are thus longitudinal waves.

Waves on a water surface:
- When a pebble is dropped in water, the water surface particles move up and down (perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation).
- These are transverse waves.
- The particles oscillate perpendicular to the direction of travel of the wave.

Difference: In sound (longitudinal), particles move parallel to wave direction. In water surface waves (transverse), particles move perpendicular to wave direction.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: WAVELENGTH (lambda):
The distance between two consecutive compressions (C) or two consecutive rarefactions (R) is called the wavelength.
SI unit: metre (m).
Represented by the Greek letter lambda (wavelength).
A peak (crest) represents maximum compression and a trough represents maximum rarefaction in the graphical representation.
FREQUENCY (nu):
The number of complete oscillations (compressions + rarefactions) per unit time is called the frequency of the sound wave.
SI unit: hertz (Hz). 1 Hz = 1 oscillation per second.
Represented by the Greek letter nu (v).
Higher frequency = higher pitch sound.
Relation: v = 1/T, where T is the time period.
TIME PERIOD (T):
The time taken by two consecutive compressions or rarefactions to cross a fixed point is called the time period.
SI unit: second (s).
Relation with frequency: v = 1/T (frequency = 1 / time period).
AMPLITUDE (A):
The magnitude of the maximum disturbance in the medium on either side of the mean value is called the amplitude of the wave.
A large amplitude = loud sound.
A small amplitude = soft (quiet) sound.
SI unit: metre (m) (for displacement amplitude); or it may be measured as pressure or density variation.
PITCH:
Pitch is how the brain interprets the frequency of a sound.
High frequency = high pitch sound (e.g., whistle, female voice).
Low frequency = low pitch sound (e.g., drum, bass guitar, male voice).
Pitch is not the same as frequency (it is the brain's perception of frequency).
LOUDNESS:
Loudness is the physiological response of the ear to the intensity of sound.
Loudness is determined by the amplitude of the sound wave.
Large amplitude = loud sound; small amplitude = soft sound.
Louder sound has higher energy and can travel a larger distance.
The SI unit of sound intensity is W/m^2; loudness is measured in decibels (dB).
QUALITY (TIMBRE):
Quality or timbre of sound is that characteristic which enables us to distinguish between sounds from different sources having the same pitch and loudness.
A sound produced by a mixture of several frequencies is called a note; it is pleasant to hear.
A sound of single frequency is called a tone.
Noise is unpleasant sound of mixed frequencies.
SPEED OF SOUND:
Speed v = wavelength x frequency, i.e., v = (lambda) x (nu).
Speed of sound remains almost the same for all frequencies in a given medium under the same physical conditions.
Speed of sound in air at 22 degrees C is approximately 344 m/s.
EXAMPLE 11.1:
Given: Frequency v = 2 kHz = 2000 Hz, Wavelength lambda = 35 cm = 0.35 m.
Find time to travel 1.5 km.
Solution:
Speed v = lambda x nu = 0.35 m x 2000 Hz = 700 m/s.
Thus, sound will take 2.1 s to travel 1.5 km.

items.question: Define wavelength of a sound wave.
items.answer: The distance between two consecutive compressions (C) or two consecutive rarefactions (R) is called the wavelength of the sound wave. It is represented by the Greek letter lambda and its SI unit is metre (m).

items.question: Define frequency of a sound wave. What is its SI unit?
items.answer: The number of complete oscillations (vibrations) per unit time is called the frequency of the sound wave. It is represented by the Greek letter nu (v). Its SI unit is hertz (Hz), where 1 Hz = 1 oscillation per second. Frequency is related to time period as: v = 1/T.

items.question: Explain amplitude. How does it affect the loudness of sound?
items.answer:
The magnitude of the maximum disturbance in the medium on either side of the mean value is called the amplitude of the sound wave. It is represented by the letter A.
Effect on loudness:
- Large amplitude: When an object vibrates with large amplitude, it creates a sound wave with large amplitude. The sound produced is loud (like striking a drum hard).
- Small amplitude: When an object vibrates with small amplitude, the sound produced is soft or quiet (like striking a drum lightly).
- A loud sound has higher energy and can travel a larger distance before dying out. Thus, amplitude determines the loudness of sound.

items.question: A sound wave has a frequency of 2 kHz and wavelength 35 cm. How long will it take to travel a distance of 1.5 km?
items.answer:
Given:
Frequency, v = 2 kHz = 2000 Hz
Wavelength, lambda = 35 cm = 0.35 m

Step 1: Find the speed of the wave.
Speed = wavelength x frequency
v = lambda x nu = 0.35 m x 2000 Hz = 700 m/s

Step 2: Find the time to travel 1.5 km.
Distance = 1.5 km = 1500 m
Time = Distance / Speed = 1500 / 700 = 15/7 s = 2.1 s

Thus, the sound will take 2.1 s to travel 1.5 km.

items.question: Distinguish between pitch and loudness of sound.
items.answer:
PITCH:
- Pitch is how the brain interprets the frequency of an emitted sound.
- The faster the vibration (higher frequency), the higher the pitch.
- High pitch sounds: whistle, female voice, child's voice.
- Low pitch sounds: drum, bass guitar, male voice.
- Pitch is related to frequency of the sound wave.

LOUDNESS:
- Loudness is the physiological response of the ear to the intensity (energy) of sound.
- Loudness is determined by the amplitude of the sound wave.
- Large amplitude = louder sound; small amplitude = softer sound.
- Louder sounds can travel greater distances.
- Loudness is measured in decibels (dB).

Key difference: Pitch is about frequency; loudness is about amplitude.

items.question: Explain the following characteristics of a sound wave: (a) Frequency (b) Time period (c) Amplitude (d) Speed and the relation between them.
items.answer:
(a) FREQUENCY (v):
- The number of complete oscillations of a particle of the medium per unit time is called frequency.
- SI unit: hertz (Hz). 1 Hz = 1 oscillation per second.
- Determines the pitch of sound - higher frequency gives higher pitch.

(b) TIME PERIOD (T):
- The time taken by two consecutive compressions or rarefactions to cross a fixed point is called the time period.
- SI unit: second (s).
- Relation with frequency: v = 1/T (or T = 1/v).

(c) AMPLITUDE (A):
- The maximum displacement (disturbance) of a particle from its mean position is called the amplitude.
- SI unit: metre (m).
- Determines loudness - large amplitude gives loud sound; small amplitude gives soft sound.

(d) SPEED (v) and its RELATION:
- The speed of sound is the distance travelled by the sound wave per unit time.
- Speed = wavelength x frequency.
- Mathematically: v = lambda x nu.
- SI unit: metre per second (m/s).
- Speed of sound in air at 22 degrees C is approximately 344 m/s.
- Speed depends on the nature and temperature of the medium; it does not change with frequency.

Relation: v = lambda x nu = lambda / T.
This shows that for a given speed, higher frequency means shorter wavelength, and lower frequency means longer wavelength.

subtopics.subtopic_name: SPEED OF SOUND IN DIFFERENT MEDIA

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Speed of sound in a medium depends on the temperature and nature of the medium.
Speed of sound decreases as we go from solid to liquid to gas (sound travels fastest in solids, slowest in gases).
At a given temperature, as temperature of the medium increases, the speed of sound increases.
Speed of sound in air at 0 degrees C = 331 m/s; at 22 degrees C = 344 m/s.
Speed of sound in air at 25 degrees C (from table): approximately 346 m/s.

Speed of sound is much less than the speed of light (3 x 10^8 m/s).
Note: The sound of thunder is heard a little later than the flash of lightning is seen, because light travels much faster than sound.

items.question: In which medium does sound travel fastest - solid, liquid, or gas? Give one example.
items.answer: Sound travels fastest in solids. For example, the speed of sound in aluminium is 6420 m/s, which is much faster than in water (1498 m/s) and in air (346 m/s) at 25 degrees C. This is because solids have greater elasticity (ability to restore shape) and the particles are more tightly packed.

items.question: How does temperature affect the speed of sound? Also explain why thunder is heard after lightning is seen.
items.answer:
Effect of temperature:
- The speed of sound increases as the temperature of the medium increases.
- At 0 degrees C, speed of sound in air is 331 m/s.
- At 22 degrees C, speed of sound in air is 344 m/s.
- Higher temperature means the particles have more energy and vibrate faster, transmitting the wave more quickly.

Thunder heard after lightning:
- Lightning and thunder are produced simultaneously during a thunderstorm.
- Light travels at approximately 3 x 10^8 m/s, while sound travels at approximately 344 m/s in air.
- Since light travels much faster than sound, we see the lightning first and hear the thunder a few seconds later.

items.question: Using Table 11.1, compare the speed of sound in different states of matter. What conclusion can you draw?
items.answer:
From Table 11.1, the speeds at 25 degrees C are:

SOLIDS (fastest):
- Aluminium: 6420 m/s
- Steel: 5960 m/s
- Iron: 5950 m/s

LIQUIDS (intermediate):
- Sea water: 1531 m/s
- Distilled water: 1498 m/s

GASES (slowest):
- Air: 346 m/s
- Oxygen: 316 m/s

Conclusion:
1. Sound travels fastest in solids, slowest in gases, and at an intermediate speed in liquids.
2. This is because the particles in solids are most tightly packed and have the strongest restoring forces (elasticity), enabling faster transmission of the wave. In gases, particles are widely spaced with weak interaction, so sound travels slowest.
3. The speed of sound varies significantly from one medium to another (e.g., steel 5960 m/s vs. air 346 m/s - about 17 times faster in steel).

sections.label: LIST OF SUB-TOPICS:
items: 11.3.3 Uses of Multiple Reflection of Sound
DEFINITION: When sound hits a surface (solid or liquid), it bounces back. This phenomenon is called reflection of sound. Sound follows the same laws of reflection as light.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Sound bounces off a solid or liquid surface just like a rubber ball bounces off a wall.
The laws of reflection of sound: (i) The incident sound, the normal, and the reflected sound all lie in the same plane. (ii) The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
An obstacle of large size (which may be polished or rough) is needed to reflect sound waves effectively.
Activity 11.5 demonstrates the reflection of sound using two pipes and a clock near a wall.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 11.5:
sections.aim: To demonstrate the reflection of sound.
sections.materials: Two identical chart paper pipes (long), a clock, a wall.
procedure: 1. Arrange two pipes on a table near a wall as shown in Fig. 11.9.
2. Keep a clock near the open end of one pipe.
3. Try to hear the sound of the clock through the other pipe.
4. Adjust the position of the pipes so that sound is best heard.
5. Measure the angles of incidence and reflection.
6. Lift one pipe vertically and observe.
sections.observation: Sound is best heard when the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. When the pipe is lifted, sound cannot be heard from the other pipe.
sections.conclusion:
Sound follows the laws of reflection - angle of incidence = angle of reflection, and both lie in the same plane.

items.question: State the laws of reflection of sound.
items.answer:
The laws of reflection of sound are:
1. The incident sound wave, the reflected sound wave, and the normal to the reflecting surface at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.
2. The angle of incidence (angle between incident sound and normal) is equal to the angle of reflection (angle between reflected sound and normal).

items.question: What is echo?
items.answer: If we shout or clap near a suitable reflecting object such as a tall building or a mountain, we will hear the same sound again a little later. This sound which we hear is called an echo. Echo is the reflection of sound by a large obstacle.

items.question: What is reverberation?
items.answer: A sound created in a big hall will persist by repeated reflection from the walls until it is reduced to a value where it is no longer audible. The repeated reflection that results in this persistence of sound is called reverberation.

items.question: What is the minimum distance required for hearing a distinct echo?
items.answer: For hearing a distinct echo, the minimum distance of the obstacle from the source of sound must be at least 17.2 m (at a temperature of 22 degrees C). This is because the sensation of sound persists in our brain for about 0.1 s, so the sound must travel at least 2 x 17.2 = 34.4 m (to the obstacle and back), requiring minimum obstacle distance of 17.2 m.

items.question: Why is the minimum time interval between the original sound and the reflected sound for hearing a distinct echo 0.1 s?
items.answer: The sensation of sound persists in our brain for about 0.1 s. If the reflected sound reaches the ear within 0.1 s of the original sound, it merges with the original sound and we cannot distinguish them separately. Therefore, for a distinct echo to be heard, the time interval between the original sound and its reflection must be at least 0.1 s.

items.question: How is reverberation in auditoriums reduced?
items.answer: Excessive reverberation in auditoriums is reduced by covering the roofs and walls with sound-absorbent materials like compressed fibreboard, rough plaster, or draperies. Seat materials are also selected based on their sound-absorbing properties. These materials absorb sound and prevent repeated reflections.

items.question: Explain with an example how echo is different from reverberation.
items.answer:
ECHO:
- Echo is a distinct, clearly heard repetition of the original sound after reflection.
- It occurs when the reflected sound reaches the ear at least 0.1 s after the original sound.
- Requires the obstacle to be at least 17.2 m away.
- Example: Shouting near a hill and hearing your voice after a short delay.

REVERBERATION:
- Reverberation is the persistence of sound due to repeated reflections from walls and ceiling in an enclosed space (hall, room).
- The reflected sounds merge with each other and the original sound, causing the sound to linger.
- Example: Speaking in a large empty hall, where voice echoes and lingers for a moment.

Key difference: Echo is a clear, distinct reflected sound heard after the original; reverberation is a prolonged, blurred persistence of sound due to multiple reflections.

items.question: Explain how the rolling of thunder is related to multiple reflections of sound.
items.answer:
During a thunderstorm, lightning is produced at a height above the earth. Thunder (the sound of lightning) is produced at a single instant. However, we hear a prolonged rolling sound of thunder rather than a single sharp crack.
This is because:
- The thunder sound is reflected from multiple surfaces - clouds, hills, trees, buildings, and the ground.
- Each reflection produces another sound wave reaching our ears at slightly different times.
- These successive or multiple reflections of the original thunder sound reach our ears one after another.
- The combined effect of all these reflections is the prolonged rolling sound of thunder we hear.
Thus, the rolling of thunder is due to successive reflections of the original sound from various surfaces at different distances.

items.question: In Activity 11.5, why can sound not be heard when one pipe is lifted vertically?
items.answer:
In Activity 11.5, when the sound travels through one pipe, it hits the wall and reflects back. To hear the reflected sound through the second pipe, the angle of incidence must equal the angle of reflection (law of reflection), and all three (incident sound, normal, and reflected sound) must lie in the same plane.
When one pipe is lifted vertically (making it perpendicular to the wall), the reflected sound is directed at a different angle (not into the second pipe). The condition for hearing the reflected sound (angle of incidence = angle of reflection, both in the same plane) is no longer satisfied. Hence, the reflected sound does not enter the second pipe and the sound cannot be heard.

items.question: A person clapped his hands near a cliff and heard the echo after 2 s. What is the distance of the cliff from the person? (Speed of sound = 346 m/s)
items.answer:
Given:
Time for echo, t = 2 s
Speed of sound, v = 346 m/s

The sound travels to the cliff and back, so total distance = v x t = 346 x 2 = 692 m.
The distance to the cliff = 692 / 2 = 346 m.

Thus, the distance of the cliff from the person is 346 m.

items.question: Why do the ceilings of concert halls and conference halls need to be curved? Explain the principle involved.
items.answer:
The ceilings of concert halls and conference halls are curved (usually concave) to ensure that sound is evenly distributed to all parts of the hall.
Principle: Reflection of sound.
- A curved ceiling acts like a curved reflector.
- When sound from the speaker/source hits the curved ceiling, it is reflected.
- A curved (concave) ceiling reflects sound uniformly in all directions, so that it reaches all corners and all seats in the hall.
- Without a curved ceiling, the sound would be concentrated in some areas and absent in others.
- A curved soundboard may also be placed behind the stage so that, after reflecting from it, sound spreads evenly across the width of the hall (Fig. 11.13).
Thus, curved ceilings use the principle of reflection of sound to ensure even sound distribution throughout the hall.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Reverberation occurs in enclosed spaces (big halls, auditoriums, cinema halls) due to multiple reflections from walls, floors, and ceilings.
Excessive reverberation in an auditorium or big hall is highly undesirable as it makes sounds unclear.
To reduce reverberation, the roof and walls of auditoriums are generally covered with sound-absorbent materials like compressed fibreboard, rough plaster, or draperies.
Seat materials are also selected based on their sound-absorbing properties.

The difference between echo and reverberation: Echo is a distinct repetition of sound heard after at least 0.1 s; reverberation is the blurring/prolonging of sound due to rapid, repeated reflections in an enclosed space.

items.question: What is reverberation? How is it different from echo?
items.answer:
REVERBERATION: The persistence of sound in an enclosed space due to repeated reflections from walls, floors, and ceilings is called reverberation. The reflected sounds arrive so rapidly (within 0.1 s) that they merge with the original sound, prolonging it.
DIFFERENCE from ECHO: In echo, the reflected sound is heard distinctly after at least 0.1 s from the original sound. In reverberation, the reflected sounds arrive rapidly (within 0.1 s) and blend with the original sound, making it unclear (not a distinct repetition).

items.question: How is excessive reverberation reduced in auditoriums? Why is it necessary to control reverberation?
items.answer:
Methods to reduce reverberation:
1. The roof and walls of auditoriums are covered with sound-absorbent materials such as compressed fibreboard, rough plaster, or thick draperies (curtains). These absorb sound energy and prevent repeated reflections.
2. The seats are made of or covered with sound-absorbent materials.
3. The floor may be carpeted.

Why necessary:
- Excessive reverberation makes sounds unclear and blurry. Words spoken by the speaker overlap with their own reflections, making it difficult for the audience to understand clearly.
- Controlling reverberation ensures that sound reaches the audience clearly and distinctly.

subtopics.subtopic_name: USES OF MULTIPLE REFLECTION OF SOUND

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: 1. MEGAPHONES AND LOUDHAILERS:
Also called horns, trumpets, and shehnais.
A tube followed by a conical opening reflects sound successively and guides most sound waves in the forward direction.
This prevents sound from spreading in all directions, making the sound louder in a particular direction.
2. STETHOSCOPE:
A medical instrument used for listening to sounds produced within the body (heart, lungs).
In a stethoscope, the sound of the patient's heartbeat reaches the doctor's ears through multiple reflections of sound inside the connecting tubes.
3. CURVED CEILINGS OF CONCERT HALLS:
The ceilings of concert halls, conference halls, and cinema halls are curved (usually concave) so that sound, after reflection from the curved ceiling, reaches all corners of the hall.
Sometimes a curved soundboard is placed behind the stage to ensure sound spreads evenly.
This ensures uniform sound distribution throughout the hall.

items.question: How does a stethoscope work? Name the principle it uses.
items.answer: A stethoscope is a medical instrument used for listening to sounds produced within the body (mainly the heart and lungs). It works on the principle of multiple reflection of sound. The sound of the heartbeat enters the stethoscope at the chest piece and travels through the connecting tubes to the earpieces by multiple reflections inside the tubes. This allows the doctor to hear the patient's heartbeat clearly.

items.question: Give three uses of multiple reflection of sound.
items.answer:
1. MEGAPHONES/LOUDHAILERS: A tube followed by a conical opening guides sound waves by multiple reflections in a particular direction without spreading it all around. Used by traffic police, soldiers, and in public announcement systems.

2. STETHOSCOPE: Sound of the patient's heartbeat or lung sounds reaches the doctor's ears through multiple reflections inside the connecting tubes of the stethoscope. Used in medical diagnosis.

3. CURVED CEILINGS OF HALLS: The curved (concave) ceilings of concert halls and auditoriums reflect sound so that it reaches all parts of the hall uniformly. Similarly, a curved soundboard behind the stage reflects sound evenly to the entire audience.

items.question: Trumpets and shehnais are musical instruments that also use multiple reflections. What is the purpose?

options.A: To reduce the loudness of the instrument
options.B: To send sound energy in a particular direction for a louder, more directed sound

items.explanation: The conical shape of trumpets and shehnais causes multiple reflections that channel sound in the forward direction, making the instrument sound louder and more directional.

items.question: In a large conference hall, a curved soundboard is placed behind the stage. How does it benefit the audience?

options.A: It reduces the frequency of the speaker's voice
options.B: It reflects sound from the speaker toward the audience, ensuring uniform distribution
options.C: It absorbs sound and prevents echo

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Average human hearing range: 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz). 1 kHz = 1000 Hz.
Children under the age of five and some animals (like dogs) can hear up to 25 kHz.
As people grow older, their ears become less sensitive to higher frequencies.
INFRASONIC SOUND (INFRASOUND): Sound of frequency below 20 Hz. Humans cannot hear infrasound.
Examples of animals using infrasound: Whales, elephants, rhinoceroses (communicate using infrasound of frequency as low as 5 Hz).
Earthquakes produce infrasound before the main shock waves, which is why some animals get disturbed before humans notice earthquakes.
ULTRASONIC SOUND (ULTRASOUND): Sound of frequency above 20,000 Hz (20 kHz). Humans cannot hear ultrasound.
Examples of animals using ultrasound: Bats, dolphins, porpoises (echolocation).
Bats produce ultrasound and use the reflected sound to detect obstacles and prey.
Moths of certain families can hear the high-frequency squeaks of bats and escape capture.
Dogs can hear ultrasound (up to 25 kHz or more).
HEARING AID:
People with hearing loss may need a hearing aid.
A hearing aid is an electronic, battery-operated device.
It receives sound through a microphone, converts it to electrical signals, amplifies the signals with an amplifier, converts back to sound with a speaker, and sends to the ear.

items.question: What is the audible range of sound for average human beings?
items.answer: The audible range of sound for average human beings is from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz). Sounds below 20 Hz (infrasound) and above 20,000 Hz (ultrasound) cannot be heard by average humans.

items.question: Define infrasound. Give two examples of animals that use infrasound.
items.answer: Sound of frequency below 20 Hz is called infrasonic sound or infrasound. Humans cannot hear infrasound. Animals that use infrasound include: (1) Whales - communicate over large distances using infrasound. (2) Elephants - use infrasound for long-distance communication. Rhinoceroses also communicate using infrasound.

items.question: Define ultrasound. Give two examples of animals that use ultrasound.
items.answer: Sound of frequency above 20,000 Hz (20 kHz) is called ultrasonic sound or ultrasound. Humans cannot hear ultrasound. Animals that use ultrasound include: (1) Bats - produce and detect ultrasound for echolocation (finding prey and obstacles). (2) Dolphins and porpoises - use ultrasound for echolocation and communication.

items.question: What is the audible range of dogs? Why can dogs hear sounds that humans cannot?
items.answer: Dogs can hear sounds up to about 25 kHz (1 kHz = 1000 Hz), which is higher than the human upper limit of 20 kHz. Dogs can hear sounds that humans cannot because they have more sensitive ears that can detect higher frequencies (ultrasound range) that are beyond human hearing capability.

items.question: How does a hearing aid work?
items.answer:
A hearing aid is an electronic, battery-operated device for people with hearing loss. It works as follows:
1. A microphone receives sound and converts it into electrical signals.
2. An amplifier amplifies (increases the strength of) the electrical signals.
3. A speaker converts the amplified electrical signals back into sound.
4. The amplified sound is sent to the ear of the user.

items.question: Why do some animals get disturbed before earthquakes?
items.answer: Before the main shock waves of an earthquake, the earth produces infrasonic sounds (frequency below 20 Hz). Humans cannot hear infrasound, but some animals like dogs, elephants, and rhinoceroses can detect these infrasonic vibrations. This is why some animals appear disturbed or agitated before humans notice an earthquake.

items.question: What is the significance of the hearing range of different organisms?
items.answer:
Different organisms have different hearing ranges, which are adapted to their environment and needs:
- Humans (20 Hz to 20 kHz): This range covers most speech and music frequencies, suitable for communication.
- Bats (ultrasound, above 20 kHz): Bats use ultrasound for echolocation - emitting high-frequency sounds and detecting the reflected echo to locate prey and navigate in the dark.
- Whales and elephants (infrasound, below 20 Hz): These animals use infrasound for long-distance communication because infrasound travels farther with less energy loss.
- Dogs (up to 25 kHz): Can hear both human speech and ultrasound, making them useful for detecting sounds humans cannot (e.g., dog whistles).
The hearing range of each animal is adapted to its ecological niche and communication needs.

items.question: Explain how bats use ultrasound for echolocation. How does this help them navigate in the dark?
items.answer:
Bats use echolocation to navigate and find food in complete darkness. The process is as follows:
1. A bat produces ultrasonic sound (very high frequency, above 20 kHz) from its mouth or nose.
2. This ultrasound travels outward and hits objects (walls, trees, insects) in the bat's path.
3. The sound reflects back from these objects.
4. The bat's sensitive ears detect the reflected sound.
5. By analysing the time delay between the emitted and reflected sound and the direction of the reflection, the bat can determine the location, distance, size, and nature of the object.
This allows bats to navigate accurately and locate prey (like insects) even in complete darkness.

items.question: What happens to human hearing as age increases? Explain why.
items.answer:
As people grow older, their ears become less sensitive to higher frequencies. In elderly people, the upper limit of hearing gradually decreases below 20,000 Hz:
- Young children can sometimes hear up to 25,000 Hz.
- By adulthood, the upper limit is typically around 20,000 Hz.
- In old age, it may drop to 15,000 Hz or even lower.
This happens because the hair cells in the cochlea of the inner ear, which are responsible for detecting sound, gradually deteriorate with age. There is no regeneration of these cells in humans. This is called age-related hearing loss (presbycusis). Additionally, prolonged exposure to loud sounds can also damage these cells and accelerate hearing loss.

items.question: Distinguish between infrasound and ultrasound. Mention one application of each.
items.answer:
INFRASOUND:
- Frequency: Below 20 Hz.
- Cannot be heard by average humans.
- Produced by: Whales, elephants, rhinoceroses, earthquakes (before main shock), large machinery.
- Application: Elephants and whales use it for long-distance communication. Scientists use infrasound detectors to detect earthquake precursors and to monitor volcanic activity.

ULTRASOUND:
- Frequency: Above 20,000 Hz (20 kHz).
- Cannot be heard by average humans.
- Produced by: Bats, dolphins, porpoises, ultrasound generators.
- Application: Bats use it for echolocation to navigate and find prey. Medical uses: ultrasonography for imaging internal body organs, detecting kidney stones, examining the foetus.

Key difference: Infrasound is below human hearing range (< 20 Hz); Ultrasound is above human hearing range (> 20,000 Hz).

items.question: A bat is flying in a dark room. Explain the complete process by which it avoids hitting the walls and finds an insect to eat, using the principle of ultrasound.
items.answer:
Process of bat echolocation:
Step 1: The bat emits a short burst of ultrasonic sound (very high frequency, above 20 kHz) from its mouth.
Step 2: The ultrasound travels through the air at approximately 344 m/s.
Step 3: When the sound wave hits the wall, the wall reflects it back as an echo.
Step 4: The bat's sensitive ears detect the reflected ultrasound (echo).
Step 5: The time delay between emission and reception of the echo tells the bat how far the wall is. Short delay = wall is close; long delay = wall is far.
Step 6: By processing multiple echoes from different directions, the bat builds a mental map of its surroundings and steers away from walls.
Step 7: When an insect is present, the insect also reflects the ultrasound. The reflection from the insect is detected, and the bat can determine the insect's position, size, and movement.
Step 8: The bat adjusts its flight path to catch the insect.
This entire process (echolocation) happens very rapidly, allowing the bat to navigate safely in complete darkness and find food.

options.B: Infrasound has longer wavelengths and loses less energy over large distances
options.D: Infrasound cannot be heard by enemies

items.explanation: Lower-frequency (infrasound) waves have longer wavelengths. They are not absorbed as much as high-frequency waves and can travel very large distances with less energy loss, making them suitable for long-distance communication.

options.B: They can detect infrasonic vibrations produced by the earth before the earthquake
options.C: They can see the earthquake approaching
options.D: They are trained to predict earthquakes

items.explanation: Before the main earthquake shock waves, the earth produces infrasonic vibrations. Animals like dogs, elephants, and snakes can detect these infrasonic waves, causing them to behave unusually before the earthquake.

options.B: Dogs hear the sound through their paws

items.explanation: Human hearing range is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. 23,000 Hz is beyond the human upper limit but within a dog's hearing range (up to about 25,000 Hz or more).

items.question: A bat emits an ultrasonic pulse and hears its echo 0.01 s later. If the speed of sound in air is 344 m/s, how far is the insect from the bat?
items.explanation: Total distance = 344 x 0.01 = 3.44 m. The insect is at 3.44/2 = 1.72 m from the bat (sound travels to insect and back).

items.question: Moths of certain families are able to escape from bats even in complete darkness. This is because:

options.B: moths are very small and bats cannot detect them
options.C: moths can hear the high-frequency ultrasound of bats and take evasive action
options.D: moths produce their own ultrasound to confuse bats

items.explanation: Certain moth families have very sensitive hearing equipment that can detect the ultrasound produced by bats. When they hear the bat's echolocation signal, they take evasive action, escaping capture.

items.question: Infrasound produced before earthquakes travels through the earth. Scientists use infrasound detectors far from earthquake zones. The best explanation for why this method works is:

options.A: Infrasound travels slower, giving scientists more time to prepare
options.B: Infrasound can travel large distances through the earth with less energy loss, alerting scientists before the main shock
options.D: Infrasound is produced only after the earthquake is over

items.explanation: Infrasound (low frequency) has long wavelengths and loses relatively little energy as it travels through the earth. This allows it to be detected at great distances before the main earthquake waves arrive, potentially giving early warning.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: PROPERTIES MAKING ULTRASOUND USEFUL:
High frequency: very short wavelengths, can detect small objects and defects.
Travels in well-defined paths even in the presence of obstacles.
Can penetrate through substances.
INDUSTRIAL APPLICATIONS:
1. CLEANING: Ultrasound is used to clean parts in hard-to-reach places (e.g., spiral tubes, electronic components, odd-shaped parts, dental instruments).
Objects are placed in a cleaning solution.
Ultrasonic waves are sent into the solution.
High-frequency vibrations cause dust, grease, and dirt to detach from the objects.
2. DETECTING CRACKS AND FLAWS IN METAL BLOCKS:
Ultrasonic waves are allowed to pass through metal blocks.
Detectors are placed on the other side to detect transmitted waves.
If there is a crack or flaw inside the metal, some ultrasound gets reflected back from the crack.
A reduced signal in the detector or a reflected echo indicates the presence and location of the defect.
Used in construction of bridges, buildings, machines (Fig. 11.14).
MEDICAL APPLICATIONS:
3. ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY:
Ultrasonic waves are made to reflect from various parts of the heart.
The reflected waves form an image of the heart.
This technique is called echocardiography.
4. ULTRASONOGRAPHY (ULTRASOUND SCANNER):
Ultrasonic waves are used to get images of internal organs (liver, gall bladder, uterus, kidney, etc.).
The waves travel through body tissue and reflect from regions where tissue density changes.
Reflected waves are converted to electrical signals, which form images on a monitor or film.
This technique is called ultrasonography.
Used to detect kidney stones, tumours, and examine the foetus during pregnancy for congenital defects.
5. BREAKING KIDNEY STONES:
Ultrasound may be used to break small stones (calculi) formed in the kidneys into fine grains.
These grains later get flushed out with urine without the need for surgery.

NOTE: Ordinary sound of longer wavelengths cannot be used for the above purposes because it would bend around corners (diffraction) and enter the detector even in the presence of defects, masking the flaw. Ultrasound, being of very short wavelength, travels in straight paths and reflects from small defects.

items.question: What is ultrasound? Give its frequency range.
items.answer: Ultrasound is sound of frequency above 20,000 Hz (20 kHz), which is beyond the upper limit of human hearing. Ultrasonic waves have very high frequency and short wavelengths. They are used extensively in industrial and medical applications.

items.question: How is ultrasound used for cleaning?
items.answer: Objects to be cleaned (e.g., electronic components, spiral tubes, dental instruments) are placed in a cleaning solution. Ultrasonic waves are sent into the solution. Due to the high frequency vibrations of the ultrasonic waves, particles of dust, grease, and dirt get detached from the objects and drop out. The objects are thus thoroughly cleaned by this method.

items.question: What is echocardiography?
items.answer: Echocardiography is a medical technique in which ultrasonic waves are reflected from various parts of the heart. The reflected waves form an image of the heart. This technique is used to detect abnormalities in the structure and functioning of the heart.

items.question: What is ultrasonography? Name two organs that can be imaged using it.
items.answer: Ultrasonography is a technique in which ultrasonic waves are used to get images of internal organs of the human body. The waves reflect from regions where tissue density changes; reflected waves are converted into images. Two organs imaged: Kidney (to detect kidney stones), Uterus (to examine the foetus during pregnancy for congenital defects and growth abnormalities).

items.question: How is ultrasound used to detect cracks in metal blocks?
items.answer: Ultrasonic waves are passed through the metal block from one side. Detectors are placed on the other side. If there is a crack or flaw inside the metal, some ultrasound is reflected back from the crack and less sound reaches the detector. The reduced signal indicates the presence of a flaw. The location of the flaw can also be determined from the position of the reflected echo.

items.question: How is ultrasound used to break kidney stones?
items.answer: Ultrasound may be directed at small stones (calculi) formed in the kidneys. The high-frequency vibrations of the ultrasonic waves break the stones into fine grains. These fine grains later get flushed out of the body along with urine, without the need for surgical removal of the stones.

items.question: Why is ultrasound preferred over ordinary sound for detecting internal defects in metal blocks?
items.answer:
Ordinary sound has long wavelengths (compared to the size of small defects/cracks). Due to its long wavelength, ordinary sound undergoes diffraction (bending around corners) and can pass around a small crack, entering the detector and masking the defect. Therefore, ordinary sound cannot reliably detect small internal cracks.
Ultrasound has very short wavelengths (due to its high frequency). It travels in very well-defined straight paths and cannot bend around small cracks. When ultrasound hits a crack or flaw, it is reflected back. The absence of signal in the detector on the other side (or the presence of a reflected echo) clearly indicates the flaw. This makes ultrasound ideal for detecting small internal defects in metal blocks.

items.question: Explain how ultrasonography (ultrasound scanner) produces images of internal organs.
items.answer:
Process of ultrasonography:
1. Ultrasonic waves (high-frequency sound above 20 kHz) are directed into the body through a probe (transducer) placed on the skin.
2. The ultrasonic waves travel through body tissues.
3. When the waves reach a region where there is a change in tissue density (e.g., boundary between two different organs, or a solid mass like a kidney stone), part of the wave is reflected.
4. The reflected ultrasonic waves return to the probe (transducer).
5. The probe converts the reflected waves into electrical signals.
6. These electrical signals are processed by a computer and displayed as images on a monitor or printed on film.
7. By analysing the images, doctors can detect abnormalities like stones, tumours, or structural defects.
This technique is safe (does not use ionising radiation like X-rays) and non-invasive.

items.question: What are the advantages of using ultrasound for medical diagnosis compared to X-rays?
items.answer:
Advantages of ultrasound over X-rays:
1. SAFETY: Ultrasound uses sound waves, which are non-ionising and harmless to body tissues. X-rays are ionising radiation that can damage cells if used too frequently or in large doses.
2. SOFT TISSUE IMAGING: Ultrasound is better at imaging soft tissues (organs like liver, kidney, uterus). X-rays are better for bones but do not image soft tissues well.
3. REAL-TIME IMAGING: Ultrasound can produce real-time moving images (e.g., observing the foetus moving in the womb, or heart beating in echocardiography). X-rays give static images.
4. NON-INVASIVE AND PAINLESS: Both are non-invasive, but ultrasound is completely safe for pregnant women and foetuses, while X-rays are avoided during pregnancy.
5. NO RADIATION RISK: Ultrasound carries no radiation risk, making it suitable for repeated use and for monitoring foetal development.

items.question: Describe the medical use of ultrasound in (a) echocardiography and (b) breaking kidney stones.
items.answer:
(a) ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY:
- Ultrasonic waves are generated and directed toward the heart.
- The waves reflect from different parts of the heart (valves, walls, chambers).
- The reflected waves are detected and converted into electrical signals.
- These signals form an image (echocardiogram) of the heart on a monitor.
- Doctors use echocardiography to assess the structure, shape, and size of the heart, detect abnormalities in valves, assess heart function (pumping), and diagnose conditions like heart failure or congenital heart disease.

(b) BREAKING KIDNEY STONES:
- When stones (calculi) form in the kidneys, they can cause severe pain and block urine flow.
- A focused beam of high-intensity ultrasound is directed at the kidney stones from outside the body.
- The high-frequency vibrations of the ultrasound waves cause the stones to vibrate intensely.
- The stones are broken into very fine grains/powder.
- These fine grains then pass out of the body naturally along with urine.
- This technique avoids the need for surgery, making it a safe and effective treatment for kidney stones.

items.question: A bridge-building company wants to check if the steel girders used in a bridge have any internal cracks. Describe the complete process they would use with ultrasound, and explain why ordinary sound cannot be used for this purpose.
items.answer:
Using ultrasound to detect internal cracks in steel girders:

PROCESS:
Step 1: An ultrasonic transmitter is placed at one end of the steel girder.
Step 2: Ultrasonic waves (frequency above 20 kHz) are sent into the girder from the transmitter.
Step 3: A detector is placed at the other end of the girder to receive the transmitted waves.
Step 4: If the girder has no cracks, the ultrasound passes straight through and is detected at full strength at the other end.
Step 5: If the girder has an internal crack or flaw, some of the ultrasound is reflected back from the crack. The signal reaching the detector on the other side is reduced.
Step 6: The position of the crack can be determined by measuring the time taken for the reflected echo to return.
Step 7: The presence and location of any crack or flaw is identified.

Why ordinary sound cannot be used:
- Ordinary sound has long wavelengths and undergoes diffraction (bends around small obstacles).
- It can bend around small cracks inside the metal and still reach the detector, hiding the defect.
- Ultrasound has very short wavelengths (due to high frequency) and travels in straight lines.
- It cannot bend around small defects - it is reflected by them.
- This makes ultrasound ideal for detecting small internal cracks that ordinary sound would miss.

options.B: Air between the probe and skin would reflect most ultrasound (large impedance mismatch); gel ensures efficient transmission of ultrasound into the body

items.question: Ordinary sound cannot be used to detect internal cracks in metal because it diffracts around them. This diffraction occurs because:

options.C: ordinary sound cannot travel in metal
options.D: ordinary sound is absorbed by metal

items.explanation: Diffraction is significant when the wavelength is comparable to or larger than the size of the obstacle/slit. The wavelength of ordinary sound (in the audible range) is much larger than typical crack dimensions in metal, so it diffracts around them. Ultrasound wavelengths are much shorter (smaller than crack dimensions), so it does not diffract and is reflected by cracks.
